newsitem.title: INDONESIA: OPINION-RIGHTS, REGULATIONS SQUEEZE JAKARTA STOCKS.
newsitem.headline: OPINION-RIGHTS, REGULATIONS SQUEEZE JAKARTA STOCKS.

text.p: Dresdner Kleinwort Benson Research
(In association with Mashill Securities, Jakarta)
JAKARTA, August 7 - The month of August sees two major events which are likely to have a negative impact on the Jakarta stock market.
These events are significant cash calls in the form of rights issue payments; and new margin finance regulations limiting domestic retail client leverage.

This report provides details of these events and argues that any impact on the index will be temporary. The momentum behind the market from enthused local investors remains fundamentally strong and we reiterate our year-end index target of 800 points.
AUGUST RIGHTS ISSUES TOTAL US$2.6 BILLION

Over the next four weeks, 6.74 trillion rupiah in rights issue payments are due to be made. This is an unprecedented amount of fund-raising by existing companies and is equivalent to 2.6 percent of the Jakarta Stock Exchange's market capitalisation of 260 trillion rupiah ($100.4 billion). This excludes cash demands made by new IPOs.
The largest come from the Sinar Mas Group's Indah Kiat raising 2.53 trillion rupiah ($975 million) and its Tjiwi Kimia subsidiary raising 587 billion rupiah ($227 million).

The other significant fund-raisers are the Lippo Group with Multipolar (754 billion rupiah - $291 million), Lippo Securities (783 billion rupiah - $302 million) and Lippo Life (951 billion rupiah - $367 million). The Lippo Group has also recently undertaken two new listings.
SINAR MAS GROUP

Minority investors have not greeted these fund-raising exercises with universal enthusiasm. Indah Kiat agreed to change the use of proceeds from pulp manufacturing to paper production in the face of investor disapproval. While this showed a degree of flexibility, it also raises questions as to the clarity of corporate strategy. The management's first priority appears to be to raise funds. The use of funds is apparently of secondary importance.
LIPPO GROUP
The rights issues by Lippo Group companies have been triggered by corporate events which had a mixed reaction from minority shareholders.

The Multipolar rights issue is being used to fund the December 1996 purchase of a 51 percent stake in department retailer Matahari. The funds raised by Lippo Securities will be used to repay amounts outstanding to the founding Riady family. This follows their sale last year of a family stake in Bank Lippo to Lippo Life, and their stake in Lippo Life to Lippo Securities. The terms of the sale last year had to be improved in response to minority shareholder concerns.
CITRA MARGA

The 500 million rupiah ($193 million) rights issue by Citra Marga coincides with the announcement that the largest founding shareholder, Yayasan Phurna Bhakti Pertiwi, has agreed to sell half its 22 percent stake.

State-owned Krakatau Steel has confirmed divestment of 2.9 percent of its nine percent stake and Indocement is considering selling down its nine percent stake. Some minority shareholders may see these actions as signalling a lack of confidence by founding shareholders in the face of the rights issue.
MARGIN FINANCE GROWS

While companies' shares are normally well-supported during the rights issue process, it is important to note that an evolving investor base means that an increasing proportion of minority investors are domestic retail clients. In turn, a growing proportion of retail investors are operating on margin finance. While there is no hard data, Mashill Securities estimates that about 25 percent of market turnover is supported by margin finance.

The leading margin finance houses in Jakarta are Mashill Securities, Lippo Securities, Trimegah Securities and Putra Saridaya Perkasa. While margin investors are exposed to a wide range of stocks, anecdotal evidence suggests that the Lippo Group stocks have been particularly favoured.
MARGIN FINANCE REGULATIONS

The introduction of margin finance regulations from August 1 may, if immediately and strictly enforced, cause disruption. The typical margin investor is probably 300 percent geared on the underlying cash deposit held by the stockbroking company (we believe that some domestic broking companies may have clients with significantly higher leverage). If the client is fully invested and is faced by a rights issue, the only options are to increase leverage or sell stock.

Investors' ability to increase leverage should be curtailed by the new regulations. Bapepam, the capital market's supervisory authority, has only issued draft regulations but we do not anticipate any dramatic changes. The main points of the regulation are:

- Brokers licensed to engage in margin finance must maintain a minimum five billion rupiah to 10 billion rupiah in net adjusted working capital. Brokers will need audited proof of this position for two months to receive a Bapepam licence.
- Margin investors must show proof of having net assets of one billion rupiah and annual income of 200 million rupiah.
- Margin investors must provide a deposit (either cash or shares) of at least 50 percent of the value of share purchases.

- If the portfolio value drops so that the ratio of the original deposit to the combined total of the initial portfolio purchase cost and accrued losses (including finance costs) falls to 35 percent, the client must increase the deposit within 90 days to take the ratio back to 50 percent.

- Stocks for which margin finance is permitted are shares which have had a daily trading value of over one billion rupiah and which have had at least 4,000 shareholders for the previous six-month period.

We believe the Jakarta Stock Exchange will enforce these regulations with relatively tight supervision although a grace period of about one month is anticipated for brokers to fall in line and to become officially licensed.
The better-managed brokers have been actively lowering clients' margin positions to fall in line with the regulations, but this may not be the case across the board.
EXPECT WEAKNESS...

The conjunction of unprecedented rights issues and a regulatory squeeze may negatively impact the index. Theoretically, this should be most evident in those stocks which have a high proportion of margin investors and which are undertaking rights issues. In the past few days, there has been noticeable weakness in Multipolar, although this may relate to concerns on the forex exposure of its Matahari subsidiary.
...TO BE TEMPORARY
We would regard any weakness as a temporary phenomenen. Much depends on how quickly Bapepam acts to penalise errant brokers.

We also believe that the momentum behind local investor interest in the stock market will continue. With market turnover having increased 134 percent last year and on track to rise by over 55 percent this year, we do not believe that this month's rights issues or new regulations will reverse this momentum.
But, like an athlete having a refreshment stop, there is a likelihood of the market taking a breather in August.

Looking forward, the margin finance regulations should significantly lower the risk of the industry and benefit the better-capitalised and managed firms. While Bapepam is lowering the risk and opportunities of margin trading, it is drafting regulations to open up and supervise new areas such as short selling. The dangers to the market, therefore, are not regulatory.
We have probably been more bullish than most in keeping our year-end net target at 800 points. Moving into 1998, we anticipate taking a more cautious approach.

We believe the government will undergo another political trial of strength six to 18 months after the presidential and vice-presidential poll next March. This could coincide with another economic wobble, such as an attack on the currency or an inflationary hike triggered, perhaps, by a poor rice harvest if the feared El Nino drought transpires.

August is likely to be a poor month but we recommend a full weighting in Indonesia until the end of this year. An element of caution should be taken as we progress into 1998, with the possibility of a buying opportunity (rather than a selling frenzy) caused by short-term political and cyclical events.
(NOTE-The views expressed in this article represent the views of the author only. They should not be seen as reflecting the views of Reuters).
